[133] [134] Intactivists further allege long-term harms, including reduced penile sensitivity, sexual dysfunction, and psychological trauma, though empirical studies on these effects remain contested and often rely on self-reported data from adults. [124] They dismiss purported medical benefits—such as lowered risks of urinary tract infections or certain sexually transmitted diseases—as insufficient to warrant routine intervention, especially given alternatives like hygiene education. [130] Specific objections target elements of brit milah like metzitzah b'peh, decrying it as a vector for disease transmission, including herpes simplex virus, based on documented infant cases in New York City between 2000 and 2011. [135]

ir.source_text:
Post-trial surveillance confirmed sustained protection, with incidence of 0.50 per 100 person-years in circumcised men versus 1.93 in uncircumcised men, and no evidence of risk compensation. [16]
[ref 16]
Male circumcision for HIV prevention in young men in Kisumu, Kenya
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17321310/
Male circumcision for HIV prevention in young men in Kisumu, Kenya pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov
No significant behavioral disinhibition, such as increased sexual partners or reduced condom use, was observed. [14] [15]

In Kisumu, Kenya, Bailey et al. randomized 2,784 men aged 18-24 years from 2002 to 2005. Over 24 months, HIV incidence rates were 2.1% (95% CI 1.2-3.0) in the circumcised group and 4.2% (95% CI 3.0-5.4) in controls, corresponding to a 51% relative risk reduction (p=0.0065). Post-trial surveillance confirmed sustained protection, with incidence of 0.50 per 100 person-years in circumcised men versus 1.93 in uncircumcised men, and no evidence of risk compensation. [16] [17]

The Rakai trial in Uganda, conducted by Gray et al. from 2002 to 2003, involved 4,996 men aged 15-49 years. After 24 months, circumcision reduced HIV incidence by 51% (adjusted incidence rate ratio 0.49, 95% CI 0.26-0.93), with rates of 0.7% in the intervention group versus 1.3% in controls among men adhering to the protocol. The trial found no increase in adverse sexual behaviors, supporting circumcision's role without compensatory risk-taking. [18] [19]

Meta-analyses of these RCTs confirm a consistent 50-60% reduction in HIV acquisition risk for heterosexual men, with protective effects persisting in long-term follow-up and no offsetting increases in transmission to female partners within trial data.

child.source_text:
No significant behavioral disinhibition, such as increased sexual partners or reduced condom use, was observed. [14] [15]

In Kisumu, Kenya, Bailey et al. randomized 2,784 men aged 18-24 years from 2002 to 2005. Over 24 months, HIV incidence rates were 2.1% (95% CI 1.2-3.0) in the circumcised group and 4.2% (95% CI 3.0-5.4) in controls, corresponding to a 51% relative risk reduction (p=0.0065). Post-trial surveillance confirmed sustained protection, with incidence of 0.50 per 100 person-years in circumcised men versus 1.93 in uncircumcised men, and no evidence of risk compensation. [16] [17]

The Rakai trial in Uganda, conducted by Gray et al. from 2002 to 2003, involved 4,996 men aged 15-49 years. After 24 months, circumcision reduced HIV incidence by 51% (adjusted incidence rate ratio 0.49, 95% CI 0.26-0.93), with rates of 0.7% in the intervention group versus 1.3% in controls among men adhering to the protocol. The trial found no increase in adverse sexual behaviors, supporting circumcision's role without compensatory risk-taking. [18] [19]

Meta-analyses of these RCTs confirm a consistent 50-60% reduction in HIV acquisition risk for heterosexual men, with protective effects persisting in long-term follow-up and no offsetting increases in transmission to female partners within trial data.

[2] By October 2023, approximately 35 million men and adolescent boys had undergone VMMC through these initiatives, representing substantial progress toward averting new infections. [57]

[120] Ethical critiques further highlight consent issues in resource-limited settings, where community pressures or inadequate counseling may coerce participation, and argue that promoting surgery ignores bodily autonomy and potential complications like infection or pain, especially when alternatives exist. [121] Groups opposing non-therapeutic circumcision extend this to VMMC, framing it as cultural imperialism rather than evidence-based policy. [10]

Rebuttals emphasize that the three pivotal RCTs (in South Africa, Kenya, and Uganda) demonstrated consistent 50-60% reduction in HIV acquisition among heterosexual men, with pooled analyses confirming biological causality via mechanisms like reduced viral entry through the foreskin. [111] Long-term follow-up from the Orange Farm trial in South Africa showed sustained 58% efficacy at 72 months, aligning with initial findings and refuting decay claims. [122] Methodological critiques are dismissed as denialism, given the trials' rigorous design, including intention-to-treat analyses and adjustments for behavior, which found no evidence of bias invalidating results. [116] [123]

On risk compensation, systematic reviews and meta-analyses of post-circumcision cohorts report no substantial increase in risky behaviors; a 2021 analysis of 28 studies found higher-quality evidence showing neutral or reduced risk profiles, with circumcised men often reporting safer practices due to counseling. Male circumcision in Africa refers to the widespread removal of the foreskin from the penis, practiced as a cultural rite of passage in many sub-Saharan ethnic groups and as a religious obligation in Muslim-majority North African societies. In sub-Saharan Africa, traditional circumcision often occurs during adolescence as an initiation into manhood, embedding social identity and masculinity norms, though it carries risks of severe complications like wound infections and deaths when performed by untrained practitioners. [1] [2] Prevalence varies regionally, exceeding 90% in North Africa due to Islamic tradition, while in sub-Saharan countries it ranges widely, with national averages around 62% but higher in certain ethnic groups. [2]

Since 2007, the World Health Organization has endorsed voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) in 15 eastern and southern African countries with high HIV prevalence, following randomized controlled trials showing approximately 60% reduction in men's risk of acquiring HIV from heterosexual sex. [3] These programs have scaled up to perform tens of millions of procedures, aiming to avert new infections, though traditional practices persist and contribute to ongoing public health challenges from botched operations. [4] Controversies surround the balance between cultural preservation and safety, with evidence of higher HIV transmission risks associated with non-medical circumcisions due to poor hygiene and delayed healing. [5] Empirical data unders

In the mid-19th century, British surgeon Jonathan Hutchinson promoted prophylactic circumcision, arguing in 1855 that it reduced syphilis transmission based on lower rates among circumcised Jewish men (2 of 111 cases) versus uncircumcised Gentiles (49 of 125). [148] [149] [150] Despite debates over causation and data accuracy, his observations influenced medical discourse, framing circumcision as a safeguard against venereal diseases amid growing public health and urban hygiene concerns. [151]

In the United States, orthopedic surgeon Lewis Sayre advanced the practice in the 1870s by associating uncircumcised foreskins with "reflex neurosis"—irritation allegedly causing spinal issues, paralysis, epilepsy, and leg weakness. [152] He cited three cases of dramatic mobility improvement after circumcision, linking results to the removal of phimotic adhesions and smegma, which he viewed as bacterial irritants. [153] Sayre's 1870 presentation to the American Medical Association and later publications extended this to prophylaxis, advocating routine newborn circumcision to prevent urinary tract problems and neuromuscular disorders, thus embedding it in U.S. pediatric surgery. [154]

ir.source_text:
Rights-based critiques frame clitoridectomy as a profound violation of bodily integrity and the right to be free from torture or cruel, inhuman treatment, as articulated in UN conventions, since it is typically inflicted on minors incapable of informed consent, perpetuating female subordination and gender-based discrimination without cultural relativism justifying harm. [103] [104] Organizations like WHO and UNICEF emphasize its incompatibility with universal human rights standards, including the Convention on the Rights of the Child, arguing it reinforces patriarchal control over female sexuality and denies equal protection under law, with over 230 million affected girls and women globally underscoring systemic rights abuses. [1] [20] Empirical assessments reveal no evidence of purported benefits like reduced promiscuity, positioning the practice as discriminatory violence rather than neutral tradition. [105] [8]

ir.source_text:
Meta-analyses of these RCTs confirm consistent efficacy of 50-60% against HIV acquisition in heterosexual men, with no evidence of behavioral risk compensation offsetting benefits. [154]
[ref 154]
Impact of male circumcision on risk of HIV infection in men ... - PubMed
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32558344/
Impact of male circumcision on risk of HIV infection in men ... - PubMed pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov
[96] A similar trial in Rakai, Uganda, involving 4,996 men aged 15-49, reported a 51% efficacy (adjusted hazard ratio 0.49; 95% CI 0.26-0.93) after 24 months, rising to 60% after excluding baseline seroconverters. The third trial, in Orange Farm, South Africa, with 3,274 men aged 18-24, showed a 61% reduction (hazard ratio 0.39; 95% CI 0.19-0.80) at interim analysis, leading to early trial termination. These results were attributed to biological mechanisms, including removal of the foreskin, which harbors Langerhans cells and CD4+ T cells susceptible to HIV entry during heterosexual intercourse, thereby reducing viral exposure and replication sites. [153]

Meta-analyses of these RCTs confirm consistent efficacy of 50-60% against HIV acquisition in heterosexual men, with no evidence of behavioral risk compensation offsetting benefits. [154] Pooled data from the three trials yielded a relative risk reduction of 0.42 (95% CI 0.31-0.57), supporting causality through intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses that controlled for confounders like sexual behavior. [151] However, these trials found no direct protective effect for female partners; a Ugandan RCT of 922 HIV-discordant couples showed no reduction in HIV transmission from circumcised infected men to uninfected women (hazard ratio 0.92; 95% CI 0.61-1.38). Indirect benefits to women via reduced community prevalence were hypothesized but not demonstrated in trial endpoints. [155]

ir.source_text:
A core motivation is the deliberate reduction of female sexual pleasure to promote premarital virginity and postmarital fidelity, distinguishing FGM from male circumcision, which lacks equivalent intent or physiological impact on pleasure. Types I and II FGM, involving clitoridectomy or excision, sever nerve-rich tissues, with clinical evidence indicating long-term dyspareunia and diminished libido in up to 70% of survivors, effects absent in male counterparts.68589-5/fulltext) This outcome aligns with explicit rationales in practicing communities, where elders cite "sealing" female desire to prevent infidelity, reinforcing male authority without reciprocal controls on men.

Relativist arguments portraying FGM as culturally empowering or analogous to Western body modifications—such as piercings or cosmetic surgeries—fail causal scrutiny, as they overlook the procedure's coercive involuntariness and subjugative ends, unlike elective adult choices. Ethnographic analyses reveal no evidence of female agency in initiations, which occur pre-puberty without informed consent, contrasting voluntary practices; instead, FGM causally entrenches dependency by linking women's social value to mutilated bodies, incompatible with individual autonomy principles. Critics of equivalence, drawing from cross-cultural data, note FGM's unique permanence and health risks (e.g., chronic infections in 20-30% of cases) as markers of control, not equivalence.

## Historical and Legislative Development

ir.source_text:
Cultural relativists argue that female genital mutilation (FGM) in Sudan functions as an adaptive cultural practice reinforcing social cohesion, family honor, and marriage eligibility within tightly knit communities, where deviation risks ostracism and economic disadvantage for girls and their kin. [58] Anthropological studies emphasize that such customs evolve from local contexts of modesty and group identity, and external prohibitions often provoke defensiveness by evoking historical impositions, such as the British colonial administration's failed 1946 ban attempt in Sudan, which fueled nationalist backlash and entrenched the practice further. [59] Relativists critique universalist interventions for hypocrisy, noting Western tolerance of analogous body modifications—like male circumcision, performed on over a million U.S. infants annually without equivalent condemnation, or elective cosmetic surgeries such as labiaplasty—while selectively targeting non-Western traditions, thereby revealing culturally biased standards rather than consistent ethical principles. [60]

In contrast, universal human rights advocates maintain that FGM constitutes a fundamental violation of bodily autonomy and dignity, transcending cultural boundaries, as affirmed by international frameworks Sudan has engaged with, including its 2006 ratification of the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW), which prohibits practices discriminating against women. [61] T

ir.source_text:
Empirical assessments refute these health-related claims, with the World Health Organization concluding that FGM confers no medical benefits and instead entails risks like hemorrhage, infection, and urinary issues without offsetting gains in hygiene or disease prevention. [2] Unlike male circumcision, which has evidence for reducing certain infections, studies find no comparable protective effects for FGM against HIV or other pathogens, with correlations sometimes cited by proponents dismissed as inconclusive due to confounding factors like overall healthcare access. [43]

A 2017 study in Nature Ecology & Evolution suggested an evolutionary angle, analyzing Demographic and Health Surveys from five West African countries and finding that, in high-prevalence ethnic groups, cut women had more surviving children by age 40, attributing this to social conformity aiding marriage and resource access. [44] Critiques highlight methodological flaws, including non-causal associations, exclusion of maternal deaths skewing fertility data, insufficient sample size across countries, and reliance on single-timepoint surveys amid declining FGM trends, rendering the findings unproven and potentially misleading for policy. [44] Social "benefits" like marriageability reflect coercive norms rather than intrinsic value, perpetuating gender control without evidence of net welfare improvement, as uncut women in low-prevalence groups show reproductive advantages. [44]

Overall, peer-reviewed consensus

[31] Swelling and edema in the affected area are also prevalent, potentially causing urinary retention or difficulty with micturition shortly after the cut. [31]

[24] Reproductive tract infections can manifest rapidly, with symptoms including fever and localized inflammation, and may progress to systemic sepsis if untreated. ### Legal and Regulatory Challenges

In New York City, regulatory efforts targeted metzitzah b'peh (MBP), the direct oral suction of blood from the circumcision wound, following reports of neonatal herpes simplex virus infections linked to the practice. Traditional circumcision rites, common in ethnic groups across Kenya, South Africa, and Zambia, often occur outside clinical settings by non-medical practitioners, leading to elevated complication rates compared to VMMC. [43] Overall, while VMMC has incrementally raised prevalence in low-baseline regions, empirical data reveal persistent heterogeneity and incomplete saturation, with traditional practices filling gaps but introducing avoidable health burdens. Redundant prepuce can lead to several potential complications, primarily stemming from impaired hygiene due to excessive foreskin coverage of the glans penis, which promotes accumulation of smegma, moisture retention, and bacterial proliferation. [27]

A common complication is recurrent balanoposthitis, an inflammation of the glans and foreskin, which occurs almost exclusively in uncircumcised males and is often linked to poor hygiene or trapped debris under the prepuce. [27] Repeated episodes of balanoposthitis may cause scarring of the foreskin, resulting in pathologic phimosis characterized by cicatricial changes that prevent foreskin retraction. [12]

Children with redundant prepuce are also at increased risk of urinary tract infections, as the excess foreskin can facilitate bacterial retention and urine stagnation. [1]

Chronic inflammation and poor hygiene have been associated with a higher risk of penile cancer, though this link is rare and often mediated by conditions such as balanitis xerotica obliterans; circumcision reduces this risk. [1] [12]

Other potential issues include buildup of smegma leading to irritation or inflammation, as well as an elevated susceptibility to certain sexually transmitted infections in adults. [1] [27]

Circumcision observance remains nearly universal among Jewish males worldwide, with rates approaching 100% in Israel across secular and religious families, reflecting its enduring role as an identity marker. [27] In the United States and elsewhere, Jewish circumcision rates similarly exceed 90%, often integrated into hospital settings while preserving ritual elements. [28] Empirical data indicate low overall complication rates for neonatal circumcision, comparable to other routine procedures, though metzitzah b'peh has been causally linked to neonatal herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) transmission. In New York City from 2000 to 2011, health authorities documented 11 cases of infant HSV-1 following ritual circumcision with oral suction, resulting in two deaths and two cases of neurological damage; further incidents occurred post-2011, prompting regulatory efforts balanced against religious autonomy. [29] [30] These risks stem from potential mohel carriage of HSV-1, an asymptomatic adult virus transmissible to infants whose immature immunity heightens severity. [31]

ir.source_text:
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends that healthcare providers inform adolescent and adult males, as well as parents of newborn boys, about the substantial evidence that male circumcision reduces the risk of HIV acquisition during heterosexual sex by approximately 60%, alongside benefits against other sexually transmitted infections; the CDC supports voluntary access without endorsing mandates. [65] Similarly, the World Health Organization (WHO) endorses voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) as part of HIV prevention strategies in high-prevalence regions, particularly sub-Saharan Africa, where over 30 million procedures have been performed since 2007, averting an estimated 615,000 HIV infections by 2020 based on modeling of randomized trial data. [38] [66]

In contrast, several European medical organizations express greater caution toward non-therapeutic circumcision in low-HIV-prevalence contexts. The Royal Dutch Medical Association (KNMG) in 2010 stated that routine circumcision violates boys' physical integrity and right to bodily autonomy, recommending deferral until informed consent can be given at adulthood due to risks outweighing unproven preventive benefits in their setting. child.source_text:
Intactivist movements, originating in the 1970s with groups like the National Organization of Circumcision Information Resources Center (NOCIRC), frame circumcision as a form of genital mutilation analogous to female genital mutilation (FGM), emphasizing the irreversible removal of the foreskin, which contains specialized nerve endings. Advocates cite histological studies documenting the foreskin's dense innervation and erogenous tissue, arguing that its excision diminishes sexual function and sensitivity, though randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have not demonstrated measurable long-term functional deficits in circumcised individuals compared to uncircumcised controls. These claims often invoke ethical precedents from bioethics literature, positing that any non-therapeutic surgery on minors prioritizes adult preferences over the child's future self-determination.

Critics of these rights-based arguments contend that intactivist rhetoric over-relies on anecdotal reports of psychological trauma and body image dissatisfaction, with empirical data from longitudinal studies showing no evidence of widespread mental health harm attributable to neonatal circumcision. records.passage:
Post-trial surveillance confirmed sustained protection, with incidence of 0.50 per 100 person-years in circumcised men versus 1.93 in uncircumcised men, and no evidence of risk compensation. [16]
[ref 16]
Male circumcision for HIV prevention in young men in Kisumu, Kenya
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17321310/
Male circumcision for HIV prevention in young men in Kisumu, Kenya pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov
No significant behavioral disinhibition, such as increased sexual partners or reduced condom use, was observed. [14] [15]

In Kisumu, Kenya, Bailey et al. randomized 2,784 men aged 18-24 years from 2002 to 2005. Over 24 months, HIV incidence rates were 2.1% (95% CI 1.2-3.0) in the circumcised group and 4.2% (95% CI 3.0-5.4) in controls, corresponding to a 51% relative risk reduction (p=0.0065). Post-trial surveillance confirmed sustained protection, with incidence of 0.50 per 100 person-years in circumcised men versus 1.93 in uncircumcised men, and no evidence of risk compensation. [16] [17]

The Rakai trial in Uganda, conducted by Gray et al. from 2002 to 2003, involved 4,996 men aged 15-49 years. After 24 months, circumcision reduced HIV incidence by 51% (adjusted incidence rate ratio 0.49, 95% CI 0.26-0.93), with rates of 0.7% in the intervention group versus 1.3% in controls among men adhering to the protocol. The trial found no increase in adverse sexual behaviors, supporting circumcision's role without compensatory risk-taking. [18] [19]

Meta-analyses of these RCTs confirm a consistent 50-60% reduction in HIV acquisition risk for heterosexual men, with protective effects persisting in long-term follow-up and no offsetting increases in transmission to female partners within trial data.

[15] Interim analysis after 473 person-years of follow-up in the intervention group and 499 in the control group revealed 20 HIV infections in the circumcision arm versus 49 in the control arm, yielding a relative risk reduction of 60% (95% CI: 32–77%), prompting early termination of the trial on ethical grounds. [15] No significant increases in sexual risk behavior were observed, and adverse events were minimal (3.8% moderate or severe complications, mostly resolving without intervention). [15]

Building on these findings, two larger RCTs reported results in early 2007. The Kenyan trial in Kisumu, led by Bailey et al., randomized 2,784 HIV-uninfected men aged 18–24 to immediate circumcision or delayed (after 24 months), with follow-up through September 2006. [17] Among 69 incident HIV cases (22 circumcised, 47 uncircumcised), circumcision conferred a 53% protective efficacy (95% CI: 22–72%; adjusted RR 0.47, 95% CI: 0.28–0.78), with no evidence of behavioral risk compensation—circumcised men reported similar or slightly fewer sexual partners and condom use rates. [2] By October 2023, approximately 35 million men and adolescent boys had undergone VMMC through these initiatives, representing substantial progress toward averting new infections. [57]

Observational studies and long-term follow-ups from the original randomized controlled trials (RCTs) conducted in Kenya, Uganda, and South Africa have corroborated the approximately 60% reduction in heterosexual HIV acquisition risk for men observed in the 2005–2007 trials. ![Celebration of the 1 millionth Voluntary Medical Male Circumcision in South Africa][float-right] Following the 2007 World Health Organization (WHO) and Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS) recommendations, voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) programs expanded rapidly in 15 priority countries in eastern and southern Africa with high HIV prevalence and low male circumcision rates. [2] By October 2023, approximately 35 million men and adolescent boys had undergone VMMC through these initiatives, representing substantial progress toward averting new infections. [57]

Observational studies and long-term follow-ups from the original randomized controlled trials (RCTs) conducted in Kenya, Uganda, and South Africa have corroborated the approximately 60% reduction in heterosexual HIV acquisition risk for men observed in the 2005–2007 trials. [12] [7] For instance, a 2020 analysis of follow-up data from a Zimbabwean cohort reported an HIV incidence of 1.2 per 100 person-years among circumcised men compared to higher rates in uncircumcised controls, with no evidence of waning protection over time. [7] Population-level data from sub-Saharan Africa have similarly associated increased VMMC coverage with reduced HIV incidence, though effects vary by region due to factors like program saturation and concurrent interventions. [97]

Male circumcision in Africa refers to the widespread removal of the foreskin from the penis, practiced as a cultural rite of passage in many sub-Saharan ethnic groups and as a religious obligation in Muslim-majority North African societies. In sub-Saharan Africa, traditional circumcision often occurs during adolescence as an initiation into manhood, embedding social identity and masculinity norms, though it carries risks of severe complications like wound infections and deaths when performed by untrained practitioners. [1] [2] Prevalence varies regionally, exceeding 90% in North Africa due to Islamic tradition, while in sub-Saharan countries it ranges widely, with national averages around 62% but higher in certain ethnic groups. [2]

Since 2007, the World Health Organization has endorsed voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) in 15 eastern and southern African countries with high HIV prevalence, following randomized controlled trials showing approximately 60% reduction in men's risk of acquiring HIV from heterosexual sex. [3] These programs have scaled up to perform tens of millions of procedures, aiming to avert new infections, though traditional practices persist and contribute to ongoing public health challenges from botched operations. records.passage:
Male circumcision in Africa refers to the widespread removal of the foreskin from the penis, practiced as a cultural rite of passage in many sub-Saharan ethnic groups and as a religious obligation in Muslim-majority North African societies. In sub-Saharan Africa, traditional circumcision often occurs during adolescence as an initiation into manhood, embedding social identity and masculinity norms, though it carries risks of severe complications like wound infections and deaths when performed by untrained practitioners. [1] [2] Prevalence varies regionally, exceeding 90% in North Africa due to Islamic tradition, while in sub-Saharan countries it ranges widely, with national averages around 62% but higher in certain ethnic groups. [2]

Since 2007, the World Health Organization has endorsed voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) in 15 eastern and southern African countries with high HIV prevalence, following randomized controlled trials showing approximately 60% reduction in men's risk of acquiring HIV from heterosexual sex. [3] These programs have scaled up to perform tens of millions of procedures, aiming to avert new infections, though traditional practices persist and contribute to ongoing public health challenges from botched operations. [4] Controversies surround the balance between cultural preservation and safety, with evidence of higher HIV transmission risks associated with non-medical circumcisions due to poor hygiene and delayed healing. records.passage:
In the mid-19th century, British surgeon Jonathan Hutchinson promoted prophylactic circumcision, arguing in 1855 that it reduced syphilis transmission based on lower rates among circumcised Jewish men (2 of 111 cases) versus uncircumcised Gentiles (49 of 125). [148] [149] [150] Despite debates over causation and data accuracy, his observations influenced medical discourse, framing circumcision as a safeguard against venereal diseases amid growing public health and urban hygiene concerns. [151]

In the United States, orthopedic surgeon Lewis Sayre advanced the practice in the 1870s by associating uncircumcised foreskins with "reflex neurosis"—irritation allegedly causing spinal issues, paralysis, epilepsy, and leg weakness. [152] He cited three cases of dramatic mobility improvement after circumcision, linking results to the removal of phimotic adhesions and smegma, which he viewed as bacterial irritants. [153] Sayre's 1870 presentation to the American Medical Association and later publications extended this to prophylaxis, advocating routine newborn circumcision to prevent urinary tract problems and neuromuscular disorders, thus embedding it in U.S. pediatric surgery. [154]

[144] However, critics contend that these findings have limited applicability to low-prevalence populations like those in the United States or Europe, where HIV transmission dynamics differ (predominantly via men who have sex with men rather than heterosexual contact), and observational studies yield inconsistent results, potentially overestimating benefits due to confounding factors such as behavioral differences. [145] [146]

Additional claimed benefits include a 10-fold reduction in urinary tract infections (UTIs) during the first year of life, with meta-analyses estimating an absolute risk reduction from 1% in uncircumcised infants to 0.1% in circumcised ones, potentially averting rare long-term renal damage. [147] Circumcision is also associated with lower risks of penile cancer (odds ratio 0.33 in meta-analysis of case-control studies) and human papillomavirus (HPV)-related outcomes, though penile cancer remains exceedingly rare (1 in 100,000 annually in developed nations), necessitating over 900 circumcisions to prevent one case when performed neonatally. [17] [148] Opponents highlight that these absolute risk reductions are marginal in hygienic contexts with access to modern sanitation and treatments like antibiotics for UTIs or HPV vaccination for cancer prevention, arguing that non-surgical interventions suffice without procedural risks. [149]

[96] A similar trial in Rakai, Uganda, involving 4,996 men aged 15-49, reported a 51% efficacy (adjusted hazard ratio 0.49; 95% CI 0.26-0.93) after 24 months, rising to 60% after excluding baseline seroconverters. The third trial, in Orange Farm, South Africa, with 3,274 men aged 18-24, showed a 61% reduction (hazard ratio 0.39; 95% CI 0.19-0.80) at interim analysis, leading to early trial termination. These results were attributed to biological mechanisms, including removal of the foreskin, which harbors Langerhans cells and CD4+ T cells susceptible to HIV entry during heterosexual intercourse, thereby reducing viral exposure and replication sites. [153]

Meta-analyses of these RCTs confirm consistent efficacy of 50-60% against HIV acquisition in heterosexual men, with no evidence of behavioral risk compensation offsetting benefits. [154] Pooled data from the three trials yielded a relative risk reduction of 0.42 (95% CI 0.31-0.57), supporting causality through intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses that controlled for confounders like sexual behavior. [151] However, these trials found no direct protective effect for female partners; a Ugandan RCT of 922 HIV-discordant couples showed no reduction in HIV transmission from circumcised infected men to uninfected women (hazard ratio 0.92; 95% CI 0.61-1.38). Indirect benefits to women via reduced community prevalence were hypothesized but not demonstrated in trial endpoints. [155]

[96] A similar trial in Rakai, Uganda, involving 4,996 men aged 15-49, reported a 51% efficacy (adjusted hazard ratio 0.49; 95% CI 0.26-0.93) after 24 months, rising to 60% after excluding baseline seroconverters. Meta-analyses of these RCTs confirm consistent efficacy of 50-60% against HIV acquisition in heterosexual men, with no evidence of behavioral risk compensation offsetting benefits. [151] However, these trials found no direct protective effect for female partners; a Ugandan RCT of 922 HIV-discordant couples showed no reduction in HIV transmission from circumcised infected men to uninfected women (hazard ratio 0.92; 95% CI 0.61-1.38). Indirect benefits to women via reduced community prevalence were hypothesized but not demonstrated in trial endpoints. [155]

records.passage:
A core motivation is the deliberate reduction of female sexual pleasure to promote premarital virginity and postmarital fidelity, distinguishing FGM from male circumcision, which lacks equivalent intent or physiological impact on pleasure. Types I and II FGM, involving clitoridectomy or excision, sever nerve-rich tissues, with clinical evidence indicating long-term dyspareunia and diminished libido in up to 70% of survivors, effects absent in male counterparts.68589-5/fulltext) This outcome aligns with explicit rationales in practicing communities, where elders cite "sealing" female desire to prevent infidelity, reinforcing male authority without reciprocal controls on men.

Relativist arguments portraying FGM as culturally empowering or analogous to Western body modifications—such as piercings or cosmetic surgeries—fail causal scrutiny, as they overlook the procedure's coercive involuntariness and subjugative ends, unlike elective adult choices. Ethnographic analyses reveal no evidence of female agency in initiations, which occur pre-puberty without informed consent, contrasting voluntary practices; instead, FGM causally entrenches dependency by linking women's social value to mutilated bodies, incompatible with individual autonomy principles. Critics of equivalence, drawing from cross-cultural data, note FGM's unique permanence and health risks (e.g., chronic infections in 20-30% of cases) as markers of control, not equivalence.

records.passage:
Cultural relativists argue that female genital mutilation (FGM) in Sudan functions as an adaptive cultural practice reinforcing social cohesion, family honor, and marriage eligibility within tightly knit communities, where deviation risks ostracism and economic disadvantage for girls and their kin. [58] Anthropological studies emphasize that such customs evolve from local contexts of modesty and group identity, and external prohibitions often provoke defensiveness by evoking historical impositions, such as the British colonial administration's failed 1946 ban attempt in Sudan, which fueled nationalist backlash and entrenched the practice further. [59] Relativists critique universalist interventions for hypocrisy, noting Western tolerance of analogous body modifications—like male circumcision, performed on over a million U.S. infants annually without equivalent condemnation, or elective cosmetic surgeries such as labiaplasty—while selectively targeting non-Western traditions, thereby revealing culturally biased standards rather than consistent ethical principles. [60]

In contrast, universal human rights advocates maintain that FGM constitutes a fundamental violation of bodily autonomy and dignity, transcending cultural boundaries, as affirmed by international frameworks Sudan has engaged with, including its 2006 ratification of the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW), which prohibits practices discriminating against women. records.passage:
Empirical assessments refute these health-related claims, with the World Health Organization concluding that FGM confers no medical benefits and instead entails risks like hemorrhage, infection, and urinary issues without offsetting gains in hygiene or disease prevention. [2] Unlike male circumcision, which has evidence for reducing certain infections, studies find no comparable protective effects for FGM against HIV or other pathogens, with correlations sometimes cited by proponents dismissed as inconclusive due to confounding factors like overall healthcare access. [43]

A 2017 study in Nature Ecology & Evolution suggested an evolutionary angle, analyzing Demographic and Health Surveys from five West African countries and finding that, in high-prevalence ethnic groups, cut women had more surviving children by age 40, attributing this to social conformity aiding marriage and resource access. [44] Critiques highlight methodological flaws, including non-causal associations, exclusion of maternal deaths skewing fertility data, insufficient sample size across countries, and reliance on single-timepoint surveys amid declining FGM trends, rendering the findings unproven and potentially misleading for policy. [44] Social "benefits" like marriageability reflect coercive norms rather than intrinsic value, perpetuating gender control without evidence of net welfare improvement, as uncut women in low-prevalence groups show reproductive advantages. [44]

Non-therapeutic infant circumcision, routine in nations like the United States (with rates around 58% as of recent hospital data) and Israel, exemplifies inherent involuntariness, as newborns cannot consent, prompting legal challenges questioning its alignment with assault statutes or rights to physical integrity. [1] [3] Proponents invoke unproven or context-specific benefits like reduced HIV transmission in high-prevalence areas, yet critics cite elevated complication risks—up to 20-fold higher in non-infants—and ethical parallels to other non-consensual body modifications. [4] [6] Debates persist over source credibility, with public health advocacy sometimes amplifying benefits while underreporting autonomy violations, reflecting institutional pressures in global campaigns. Infection poses an acute risk owing to the use of unsterilized instruments and non-aseptic conditions typical of traditional settings. [24] Reproductive tract infections can manifest rapidly, with symptoms including fever and localized inflammation, and may progress to systemic sepsis if untreated. [24] Tetanus infection is a further concern from contaminated blades, contributing to immediate morbidity in vulnerable populations. [31]

### Legal and Regulatory Challenges

In New York City, regulatory efforts targeted metzitzah b'peh (MBP), the direct oral suction of blood from the circumcision wound, following reports of neonatal herpes simplex virus infections linked to the practice. Between 2000 and 2011, health officials documented 24 cases, including two fatalities, prompting the New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene to enact Section 181.21 of the Health Code in September 2012, requiring mohels to obtain signed parental consent acknowledging MBP risks before performing it. Traditional circumcision rites, common in ethnic groups across Kenya, South Africa, and Zambia, often occur outside clinical settings by non-medical practitioners, leading to elevated complication rates compared to VMMC. Studies across African contexts document adverse events like infections, excessive bleeding, and penile injuries at rates exceeding 10–20% in traditional procedures versus under 2% in medical ones, per WHO-monitored data. [44] [44] This disparity underscores causal risks from inadequate sterilization and post-operative care in non-clinical environments, prompting shifts toward regulated medical alternatives in program areas. [43] Overall, while VMMC has incrementally raised prevalence in low-baseline regions, empirical data reveal persistent heterogeneity and incomplete saturation, with traditional practices filling gaps but introducing avoidable health burdens. [9]

records.passage:
Redundant prepuce can lead to several potential complications, primarily stemming from impaired hygiene due to excessive foreskin coverage of the glans penis, which promotes accumulation of smegma, moisture retention, and bacterial proliferation. [27]

A common complication is recurrent balanoposthitis, an inflammation of the glans and foreskin, which occurs almost exclusively in uncircumcised males and is often linked to poor hygiene or trapped debris under the prepuce. [27] Repeated episodes of balanoposthitis may cause scarring of the foreskin, resulting in pathologic phimosis characterized by cicatricial changes that prevent foreskin retraction. [12]

Children with redundant prepuce are also at increased risk of urinary tract infections, as the excess foreskin can facilitate bacterial retention and urine stagnation. [1]

Chronic inflammation and poor hygiene have been associated with a higher risk of penile cancer, though this link is rare and often mediated by conditions such as balanitis xerotica obliterans; circumcision reduces this risk. [1] [12]

Other potential issues include buildup of smegma leading to irritation or inflammation, as well as an elevated susceptibility to certain sexually transmitted infections in adults. [1] [27]

records.passage:
Circumcision observance remains nearly universal among Jewish males worldwide, with rates approaching 100% in Israel across secular and religious families, reflecting its enduring role as an identity marker. [27] In the United States and elsewhere, Jewish circumcision rates similarly exceed 90%, often integrated into hospital settings while preserving ritual elements. [28] Empirical data indicate low overall complication rates for neonatal circumcision, comparable to other routine procedures, though metzitzah b'peh has been causally linked to neonatal herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) transmission. In New York City from 2000 to 2011, health authorities documented 11 cases of infant HSV-1 following ritual circumcision with oral suction, resulting in two deaths and two cases of neurological damage; further incidents occurred post-2011, prompting regulatory efforts balanced against religious autonomy. [29] [30] These risks stem from potential mohel carriage of HSV-1, an asymptomatic adult virus transmissible to infants whose immature immunity heightens severity. [31]

### Islam

In Islam, male circumcision, known as khitan, is regarded as part of the fitrah—the innate human disposition—based on a hadith narrated by Abu Hurayra in which the Prophet Muhammad stated, "Five acts are part of the fitrah: circumcision, shaving the pubic hair, trimming the mustache, clipping the nails, and plucking the armpit hair."
